alt: Five numbered steps of a body paragraph: claim, lead-in, evidence, commentary and link. Beside them a bar shows a timed-essay paragraph in which lead-in and evidence share one sentence and commentary takes about half the space.
caption: Claim, lead-in, evidence, commentary, link: a starting point, not a formula.

after: ## Three ways to use a source
alt: Bars compare a source passage with three ways of using it: a quotation copies exact words, a paraphrase restates the idea in new words at about the same length, and a summary condenses it to the main point. Each has a use and a danger, and all must credit the source and connect to the claim.
caption: Quote for wording, paraphrase for the idea, summarise for the gist.

after: ## Embedding: weaving a quotation into your own sentence
alt: A dropped quotation, “With malice toward none, with charity for all”, sits alone between a claim and a vague comment. In the embedded version the phrases “malice toward none” and “charity for all” sit inside the writer’s own sentence about shifting from vengeance to reconciliation. Four embedding techniques are listed below.
caption: An embedded quotation reads as part of your argument, grammatically and logically.

after: ## Signal verbs and what they tell the reader
alt: Five groups of signal verbs and what they suggest: states, notes and observes for a neutral report; urges and calls on for action; warns and cautions for a risk; concedes and admits for granting a point; insists and maintains for a strongly held claim. Notes warn against “proves” and “shows” when the source only suggests or opines.
caption: “Says” is neutral; verbs like “urges” or “concedes” show the writer’s stance.

after: ## Worked example 1: from dropped quotation to embedded evidence
alt: The strong paragraph about Lincoln’s Second Inaugural split into four parts: a claim in the writer’s own words, a quotation embedded as the object of “proceed”, a second quotation introduced after a colon, and commentary on the words “work” and “strive”. A note suggests covering the quotations to test the paragraph.
caption: Claim, embedded evidence and commentary on single words: no evidence left unexplained.
